newsitem.title: JAPAN: SESC to recommend Nomura penalty next week-sources.
newsitem.headline: SESC to recommend Nomura penalty next week-sources.

text.p: Japan's securities watchdog, the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC), is likely to make recommendations to the finance minister on penalties against Nomura Securities Co Ltd as early as next week, government sources said on Thursday.
The finance minister would then impose administrative penalties on Japan's top brokerage at the end of July or in early August, they said.
The financial markets are speculating that the Finance Ministry may suspend part of Nomura's business for up to six months.
Under Japan's securities law, administrative penalties can be imposed only after the securities watchdog makes recommendations to the finance minister.

Former Nomura executives, including former president Hideo Sakamaki, and Nomura itself are expected to face harsh penalties after being indicted on charges of violating the Securities and Exchange Act by compensating a firm run by Yoshinori Koike, younger brother of "sokaiya" racketeer Ryuichi Koike.

Following Tokyo prosecutors' indictment of Nomura and Sakamaki for a second time on Wednesday, the sources said the SESC is highly likely to recommend action to the finance minister on either Tuesday or Friday of next week.
The SESC lacks the legal authority to take punitive action itself but can recommend that the finance minister mete out administrative penalties.
A spokesman at the SESC told Reuters that the securities watchdog could not comment on the exact timing of the action, but said it held meetings every Tuesday and Friday.

On Wednesday, Sakamaki and former Nomura managing director Nobutaka Fujikura were charged with conspiring with other Nomura officials to pay 320 million yen in cash to Ryuichi Koike around March 24, 1995.
Sakamaki was arrested in late May and indicted on other charges in June in connection with alleged payments of 49.73 million yen to Koike in 1995.
Nomura was also indicted in June on charges of illegally compensating a company owned by Ryuichi Koike's brother for trading losses.

Sokaiya extort money from companies by threatening to disclose management misdeeds or disrupt annual shareholders' meetings. Payoffs to such corporate extortionists have been illegal since 1983 but the practice has continued.
